title: Silence as Communication
hook: Between men who know each other well, silence can carry more than talk: comfort, respect, anger, or a question nobody wants to ask out loud.
why:
Men are often accused of not talking, and sometimes the accusation is fair. But a great deal of what passes between men passes in silence: the hour on a riverbank without a word, the quiet in the car after a funeral, the silence that falls when a friend says something that matters and nobody knows what to say. There is also the other kind: the stony silence in an argument, the silent treatment that lasts for days, the silence of a man who has stopped trying to be heard.

The chapter on voice in Part I treated pauses as the sound of thinking. This chapter treats silence as a message in its own right. It covers what brief silences do to a group, how silence can comfort and why some cultures fall silent at exactly the moments others rush to talk, the comfortable silence of old friends, the stonewalling that damages relationships and why it often happens, the silent treatment as punishment, how to tell one silence from another, and how to hold a silence well.

teach.p:
In 2011 Namkje Koudenburg, Tom Postmes and Ernestine Gordijn asked people to imagine themselves in a conversation, or to watch a video of three people talking, in which the talk either flowed smoothly or was interrupted by a silence of just four seconds. People who experienced the silence reported feeling less self-assured, more rejected and less like they belonged, and some of them had not even noticed that it had happened.

The finding captures something everyone knows. A gap in conversation is felt before it is thought about. In a group, a brief silence after someone speaks can feel like a verdict on what they said. Koudenburg's later research found that when a group fell silent after someone expressed an opinion, people who badly wanted to belong tended to shift their opinion toward the group's.

But the meaning of a silence depends entirely on the setting and the relationship. The four-second gap that feels like rejection among new colleagues may feel like nothing at all between two old friends fishing, and like comfort between two men at a graveside. Silence is a blank that each person fills with what they expect.

That is why reading silence is so hard and so important. The figures here sit together on a bench, not speaking. Whether this is the easy quiet of friends, the tense quiet after an argument, or the heavy quiet of grief cannot be told from the silence itself. It has to be read from everything around it.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if brief silences had no effect on how people felt about a conversation. Koudenburg and colleagues found that they did, though in imagined and watched conversations rather than live ones, so effects in real conversation may be weaker or stronger.

teach.p:
In 1970 the anthropologist Keith Basso described the situations in which Western Apache people in Arizona chose to say nothing. They kept silent on meeting strangers, in the early stages of courtship, when children returned home after a long absence, when someone was shouting at them in anger, when they were with people who were grieving, and during curing ceremonies. Basso's explanation was that silence was the proper response to situations in which relationships were uncertain or unpredictable. With a grieving person, words could wound, and the right thing was to be present and quiet.

Many Western men would recognise the instinct, even if their culture tells them that silence in such moments is awkward. A man sitting with a friend who has just lost his father often feels he should say something and has nothing to say. Basso's account suggests that the silence may itself be the right thing, provided it is a silence of presence rather than absence.

The difference shows in the body. A comforting silence stays near: it sits beside, looks at the same thing, breathes slowly, perhaps rests a hand on a shoulder. It does not check a phone, look at the door or fidget. It says I am here, and I am not going anywhere, without the risk of saying the wrong thing.

The figures here stand together, heads bowed, saying nothing. At a funeral, this is often the most eloquent thing three men can do. The chapter on mourning together at the end of this part returns to it.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if silence in the presence of grief were always experienced as abandonment. For some grieving people it is, which is why a comforting silence must stay physically present and be broken when the other person wants to talk.

teach.p:
Among the clearest signs of a close friendship is the ability to be silent together without strain. Two old friends on a long walk may go twenty minutes without speaking, and both will describe it afterwards as a good walk. Two new acquaintances in the same silence would be searching for something to say within seconds.

You can usually tell the difference by watching. In a comfortable silence, bodies are relaxed and still. Breathing is slow and even. Both people tend to look at the same thing, or at nothing in particular, rather than at each other. When talk resumes, it does so easily, often on a new subject, with no sense of having rescued the moment.

In an awkward silence, the body works. People fidget, shift, touch their faces, glance at each other and away, check phones. Breathing becomes shallow. When talk resumes, it comes with a little burst of relief or a forced topic, and someone may laugh at nothing. Koudenburg's findings suggest why: an awkward silence feels like a threat to belonging, and the body treats it as one.

For a reader, the ease of a shared silence is a useful measure of a relationship. If you and a friend can no longer be quiet together without strain, something may have changed between you. The figures here walk side by side, in step, saying nothing. The rhythm of their walking does the talking.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if the ease of shared silence bore no relation to how close two people were. The claim rests on observation and on research on conversational flow rather than on direct measurement of friends' silences, so treat it as a useful heuristic.

teach.p:
The psychologist John Gottman, who spent decades studying couples in conflict, identified stonewalling as one of four behaviours that predict the breakdown of a relationship. A stonewaller withdraws from the conversation: he goes silent, his face becomes still, he looks away or down, he stops giving the small nods and sounds that show he is listening. To the other person, he seems to have turned to stone, and it feels like contempt or indifference.

Gottman reported that in his studies, roughly 80 to 85 per cent of stonewallers were men. He also found that stonewalling often follows what he called flooding: a state of physical overwhelm during conflict, often marked by a heart rate above about 100 beats a minute, in which a person can no longer think clearly or listen. On this account, the stonewaller is not indifferent at all. He is overwhelmed, and silence is his attempt to stop the flood.

That does not make stonewalling harmless; it still leaves the other person shut out. But it changes the remedy. Gottman's advice is to recognise flooding, say so, and take a real break of at least twenty minutes, doing something calming rather than rehearsing the argument, before coming back to it. The chapter on disagreement later in this part builds on this.

The figure here has turned away, arms hanging, face hidden. In an argument, this posture is often read as I do not care. It may mean I cannot cope right now. Only he can tell you which, and he may need twenty minutes before he can.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if stonewalling were usually a calm, deliberate choice rather than a response to overwhelm. Gottman's observations support the flooding account, though his figures come from his own studies of couples rather than from independent replications.

teach.p:
There is another kind of silence that does deliberate harm. The silent treatment, refusing to speak to someone as a punishment, is a form of what psychologists call ostracism, and the psychologist Kipling Williams has spent a career showing how much it hurts.

In one of the best-known studies, published in 2000, Williams, Christopher Cheung and Wilma Choi had people play a simple online game of catch with two other players they would never meet. In one version, the other players simply stopped throwing the ball to them after a few throws. Even this trivial exclusion, by strangers, over a computer, lowered people's mood and their sense of belonging and control. The game, called Cyberball, has since been used in hundreds of studies with similar results.

If being left out of a game by strangers stings, being frozen out for days by a partner, a father or a friend hurts a great deal more. The silent treatment can feel safer to the person giving it than an argument, but to the person receiving it, it often feels like being erased.

It is worth distinguishing the silent treatment from needing space. Saying “I need an hour on my own, then I'll come and find you” is a silence with a door left open. Refusing to speak, with no explanation and no end in sight, is a silence with the door locked. The figures here stand turned away from each other. Whether this is a pause or a punishment depends on whether either of them has said when it will end.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if being ignored had little effect on people. The Cyberball research consistently finds that it does, though laboratory exclusion is far milder than the silent treatment in real relationships.

teach.p:
When a man falls silent, the question is which silence you are hearing. The rivals are many: comfort, thought, grief, fatigue, comfortable familiarity, disagreement held back, flooding, punishment, depression, or simply nothing to say. Reading them uses everything this book has covered.

Look at the breath: slow and even, held, or quick and shallow. Look at the posture: settled, braced, collapsed or turned away. Look at the face and gaze: relaxed and wandering, fixed on a point, avoiding you, or closed. Look at the hands: still, fidgeting, gripping. And look at what came before: a question he did not want to answer, a remark that stung, a long day, a piece of bad news.

Compare it with his baseline. Some men are naturally quiet, and their silence carries less than another man's. Some cultures place more value on silence in conversation than others, and some neurodivergent people find conversation tiring and need quiet to recover. A silence that is out of character is more informative than one that is not.

When in doubt, check lightly. “Quiet one tonight?” or “You've gone quiet; are you all right?” gives him an easy way to tell you, and an easy way to say he is fine. The figure here sits still, hands clasped in his lap. He might be calm, or holding himself very carefully together. His silence alone will not tell you which.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if different kinds of silence looked the same in the body. They often overlap, which is why the reading must draw on context and baseline and be checked with a question.

teach.p:
Holding a silence is a skill, and most people are poor at it. The commonest mistake is to fill it. A friend says something hard, and the listener rushes in with advice, reassurance or a story of his own, because the silence feels unbearable. The friend, who was perhaps about to say more, stops.

After you ask a real question, wait. Count slowly to ten in your head if you need to. Keep your body still and near, your breath slow, your eyes on something other than his face if you are side by side. Many men need the silence to find the words, and the words that come after it are often the important ones.

With grief, let the silence be company, and let him break it. With anger, give space, but say when you will be back, so that your silence is a pause rather than a punishment. In an argument, if you feel yourself flooding, say so before you go quiet: “I'm getting overwhelmed; I need twenty minutes, and then I want to finish this.”

And explain your own silences when they might be misread. “I'm quiet because I'm thinking about what you said, not because I'm annoyed” costs a sentence and prevents an hour of worry. The figures here sit side by side on a bench. One of the most generous things a man can do for another is to sit beside him in silence and not need it to end.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if filling silences helped people say difficult things. Experience in counselling and conversation research suggests the opposite, though some people find long silences uncomfortable and need a gentle prompt.
teach.pullQuote: Sit beside him in silence, and do not need it to end.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Reaching for a phone in a pause
poseGallery.annotation: A phone in a pause says that the silence is empty. Staying still and near says that it is shared.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Going silent and turning away mid-argument
poseGallery.annotation: Stonewalling shuts the other person out even when it is really overwhelm. Name it, take a real break, and come back.
A silence that punishes locks the door. A silence that keeps company leaves it open.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Filling every pause across the table
poseGallery.annotation: Between friends, silence side by side can feel easy. Across a table, the same silence often feels like a question demanding an answer.

poseGallery.doCaption: Waiting for the quiet voice to finish thinking
poseGallery.dontCaption: A meeting that fills every pause
poseGallery.annotation: Some people need a few seconds before they speak; rushing in takes their turn away. Waiting gives it back.

poseGallery.doCaption: Sitting near him, saying nothing, staying
poseGallery.dontCaption: A man gone silent after bad news, left alone
poseGallery.annotation: After bad news, silence can be the right response. Company without questions tells him he is not alone with it.

caseStudy:
Martin, fifty-two, and his wife Claire have the same argument every few months, about money. It goes the same way each time. Claire raises something, Martin answers briefly, Claire presses, and Martin goes silent. He sits very still, stares at the table, and stops responding. Claire reads it as contempt and gets louder. Eventually Martin leaves the room, and they do not speak for a day.

After one of these arguments, Claire shows Martin an article about stonewalling and flooding. He reads it twice. The description of his own experience, the pounding heart, the sense of being unable to think, the urge to shut down, is so exact that he is embarrassed. He had always thought of his silence as keeping the peace.

They agree on a signal. When Martin feels himself flooding, he will say, “I need twenty minutes,” go for a walk, and come back to finish the conversation. The first time, he comes back after forty minutes and apologises for the extra twenty. The conversation that follows is the best they have had about money in years.

That spring, Martin's father is dying in a hospice. Martin visits every evening and sits by the bed for an hour, mostly in silence, his hand on the blanket near his father's. His father, who never talked much either, sometimes opens his eyes and looks at him, and Martin nods.

At the funeral, his brother says that their father told the nurses those evenings were the best part of his day. Martin realises that he has known two very different silences his whole life, and has only lately learned to tell them apart.
observe: Notice the next silence in a group conversation, how long it lasts, and what people do with their bodies during it.
Notice which of your friends you can be silent with comfortably, and which you cannot.
Notice your own silences in disagreement: when you go quiet, what is happening in your body?
Notice a silence that someone explains, and one that nobody explains, and how each one feels.

drills.name: Count to Ten
steps: In your next real conversation, after you ask a question that matters, count slowly to ten in your head before saying anything else.
Keep your body still and your breathing slow while you count.
Notice whether the other person fills the silence, and what they say.
Afterwards, write down what came after the silence.
variations: Try the count in a meeting rather than a one-to-one conversation, after asking the group a question.
Notice how long you can wait before you feel the urge to speak, and whether it changes with practice.

drills.name: Flooding Map
steps: Recall the last time you went silent in an argument.
Write down what was happening in your body: heart, breath, face, hands, thoughts.
Write down how the other person read your silence, if you know.
Write the sentence you could have said instead, such as “I need twenty minutes, then I want to finish this.”
Decide what you would do in those twenty minutes that would actually calm you.
variations: Ask the person you argue with most what your silence looks like to them, and listen without defending yourself.
Plan exactly where you will go and what you will do in your twenty minutes, so that the break actually calms you.

drills.name: Silent Company
steps: Spend twenty minutes with a friend or family member doing something side by side in silence: a walk, a drive, fishing, a job.
Agree beforehand, if it helps, that you do not need to talk.
Notice the moments when you feel the urge to fill the silence, and what your body does.
Afterwards, ask how it was for the other person.
Write down whether the silence felt comfortable, awkward or something else.
variations: Try silent company with someone you are less close to, and compare how the silence feels.
Try a silent walk with a friend, and notice whether conversation comes more easily afterwards.

drills.name: Explain a Silence
steps: For one week, whenever you go quiet in a way that might be misread, explain it in a sentence.
Use simple words, such as “I'm quiet because I'm thinking, not because I'm cross.”
Notice how people respond to the explanation.
At the end of the week, note whether any misunderstandings were avoided.
variations: Explain one silence to someone at work this week, and one at home, and compare the responses.
Ask a quiet friend what explanation they would like others to give them when they go quiet.

quiz.q: During an argument, a man goes silent, stares at the table and stops responding. What does Gottman's research suggest is often going on?
options: He has stopped caring about the relationship and is showing it
He is calmly deciding how best to win the argument when he speaks
He may be physically overwhelmed and shutting down to cope
He is waiting politely for his partner to finish what she has to say
quiz.explain: Gottman found that stonewalling often follows flooding, a state of physical overwhelm in which listening becomes hard. It still shuts the other person out, but the remedy is a real break and a return, not a judgment of indifference.

quiz.q: What did Koudenburg and colleagues find about a four-second silence in a conversation?
options: People felt more rejected and less as if they belonged, even unnoticed
People felt more relaxed, because the silence gave them time to think
The silence had no effect unless it lasted at least half a minute
Only people who noticed the silence were affected by it at all
quiz.explain: A brief disruption to the flow of conversation left people feeling less self-assured and more rejected, even when they had not noticed it. A silence is felt before it is thought about.

quiz.q: According to Keith Basso, when did Western Apache people tend to fall silent?
options: Only when they were angry with someone and wished to punish that person by withholding speech
In uncertain situations, such as meeting strangers or being with the grieving
Whenever they were speaking with someone older or more senior
Only during formal religious ceremonies, never in daily life
quiz.explain: Basso described silence as the proper response to situations where relationships were uncertain, including meeting strangers and being with people in grief. In those moments, silence was a form of respect and presence.

quiz.q: A man feels himself flooding during a row. What does Gottman's advice suggest he do?
options: Push through and keep talking until the whole argument is resolved, however long it takes
Go quiet and leave the room, then avoid the subject in future
Raise his voice, so that the other person stops and listens to him
Say he is overwhelmed, take a break of twenty minutes or more, then return
quiz.explain: Naming the flooding, taking a real break that is actually calming, and coming back to finish the conversation turns a stonewall into a pause. Leaving with no return turns it into the silent treatment.

quiz.q: What did the Cyberball studies show about being ignored?
options: Even brief exclusion by strangers in a game lowered mood and belonging
People felt nothing when ignored, as long as the others were strangers
Being left out of the game raised people's self-esteem, oddly enough
Exclusion only hurt when it came from close friends or family members
quiz.explain: Being left out of a simple online game of catch by strangers was enough to lower mood and sense of belonging. The silent treatment from someone close is a far stronger version of the same harm.

quiz.q: You ask a friend how he is coping since his divorce. He goes quiet and looks out of the window. What fits this chapter best?
options: Fill the silence quickly with reassurance, so that he is not uncomfortable
Change the subject at once, since the silence shows he does not want to talk
Stay near and still, and wait, giving him time to find the words
Ask him three more questions in a row, so that he has to answer one of them
quiz.explain: Silence after a real question is often the time a man needs to find his words. Staying near and patient lets the next sentence come, and he can still choose not to answer.

quiz.q: How did Keith Basso explain the Western Apache practice of falling silent in certain situations?
options: Silence suited situations in which relationships were uncertain or unpredictable
Silence was a punishment used against anyone who had broken the community's rules
Silence was simply a sign that the Apache people had less to say than other groups
Silence was required only during ceremonies and was never used in everyday life
quiz.explain: Basso argued that Western Apache people fell silent in situations where relationships were uncertain or unpredictable, such as meeting strangers or being with the grieving. Silence there was a form of respect.

quiz.q: A thoughtful new colleague pauses for several seconds before answering questions in meetings, and others keep jumping in. She has started saying little. What fits this chapter best?
options: Keep answering for her, since a long pause clearly means she does not know
Ask her to speak faster so that meetings can move along more quickly
Wait through her pauses, and ask the team to leave her room to finish
Stop asking her questions in meetings and send them to her by email
quiz.explain: A pause before answering is often thought rather than uncertainty. Filling it takes her turn away. Waiting, and helping the team wait, lets her speak.

quiz.q: Someone says that refusing to speak to a partner for a few days is a harmless way to cool off after a row. What does this chapter say?
options: It is right, since silence always helps both people calm down
Used as punishment it hurts; a named, time-limited break is different
It is right, but only if both partners agree never to mention the row again
It is wrong, since any silence during a disagreement is a sign of abuse
quiz.explain: Williams's research shows how much being ignored hurts. A break that is named and has an end, "I need twenty minutes", is very different from silence used to punish.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific silence in your life that mattered: a silence that comforted you, one you used to shut someone out, or one that someone used on you. Describe the setting, what the bodies were doing, and how long it lasted. What did the silence mean to each person, and did they read it the same way? If it was a silence you created, what would you say now to make its meaning clear?
reflection.guidance: Silences are easy to remember by their feeling and hard to remember by their details, so try to recall the posture, breath, gaze and hands. If the silence was a stonewall or a silent treatment, be honest about what was happening in your body at the time. The point is not to judge yourself but to learn which silences you use, and how they land.

failureMode: The first failure is to treat silence as empty, when even a four-second gap can make people feel rejected. The second is to fill every silence, rushing in with advice or stories just as a man was about to say what mattered. The third is to read a stonewall as contempt without considering flooding, or, if you are the one stonewalling, to leave the other person shut out without naming what is happening and coming back. The fourth is to use silence as punishment, freezing someone out with no explanation and no end, which research on ostracism shows does real harm. And the fifth is to leave a grieving friend alone because you have nothing to say, when your silent presence would have been enough.

moreCases.title: The drive home from the funeral
moreCases.scene:
Liam, thirty-eight, and his younger brother Sean, thirty-five, drive home together after their father's funeral, two hours up the
  motorway. For the first ten minutes, Liam talks: about the service, about which relatives turned up and which did not, about the food at the
  wake, about the arrangements for clearing their father's flat. Sean answers in single words, looking out of the side window. Liam talks more, and
  then turns the radio on, and then off again, and asks Sean whether he is all right. Sean says he is fine.

  By the time they reach the motorway, Liam has decided that Sean is angry with him. Perhaps it was the eulogy, which Liam gave and Sean did not.
  Perhaps it was something about their father's will. He goes quiet himself, hurt, and the silence in the car becomes tense.

  At a service station, Sean says, without looking at him, "I just wanted it to be quiet for a bit, Liam. That's all."

Liam had been talking all day, organising, greeting, thanking people for coming, giving the eulogy. He had not cried once. In the car, the talk simply kept coming, as if stopping would let something else in.

Sean has not cried either. At the graveside, he stood very still with his hands clasped in front of him, and when the coffin was lowered, he looked at the trees. Liam noticed it at the time and thought it meant Sean was coping better than he was.
moreCases.misread:
Liam read Sean's silence as anger directed at him, because he found the silence unbearable and needed a reason for it. His own talk had been his way of coping, and he assumed that Sean's silence was a reaction to it.

And by going quiet himself, hurt, he turned Sean's grief-silence into a mutual one with a different meaning, which made the car feel colder than either of them intended.

He also took his own coping style as the right one. For Liam, talking made the grief bearable. It did not occur to him that the same talk might make it unbearable for his brother.

Sean's silence was also not new. He had always been the quieter brother. Against that baseline, a quiet drive after a funeral was even less likely to be about Liam.
moreCases.betterRead:
Silence is never nothing, and Koudenburg's research shows how quickly even a short gap makes people feel rejected. But Basso's study of Western Apache silence described something many cultures share: that silence is often the right response to grief, when words feel too small. Sean's looking out of the window, his single words and his stillness could fit anger, but they fit grief at least as well, and the setting, an hour after their father's burial, made grief far more likely. Liam's talking and his radio were attempts to fill a silence that Sean needed. A better reading would have weighed the setting and offered the quiet rather than resisting it: "Do you want a bit of quiet? That's fine." After the service station, they drove the rest of the way in silence, and it changed. By the last half hour, it felt to Liam like the two of them sharing something. When they reached Sean's house, Sean put his hand on Liam's arm for a moment before he got out.

Liam also told Sean, much later, that the silence in the car was one of his best memories of that week. Sean said it was one of his too.

moreCases.title: The silence that punished
moreCases.scene:
Gareth, forty-six, discovers that his son Jake, fifteen, has lied to him about where he was on Saturday night: not at a friend's house, as he
  said, but at a party where there was drinking. Gareth is furious and frightened. He decides that the most powerful punishment is silence. For four
  days he does not speak to Jake, does not look at him at meals, and answers his questions, if at all, by speaking to Jake's mother. Gareth's own
  father did this to him, and he remembers how effective it was.

  By the third day, Jake has stopped eating breakfast with the family. He spends the evenings in his room. On the fourth day, his mother finds him
  crying, and he says that his dad hates him.

  Jake's mother tells Gareth that this has gone far enough. Gareth says that Jake needs to learn that lying has consequences.

Gareth's wife has tried twice to talk to him about it. Both times he said that he was handling it, and that Jake needed to see that his father meant business.

Jake has also started sleeping badly. His mother hears him up at two in the morning, and on the fourth day his form tutor rings to say that he seemed distracted and fell asleep in a lesson.

Gareth has also caught himself glancing at Jake at dinner, wanting to say something, and stopping, because he has decided that speaking first would mean losing.
moreCases.misread:
Gareth read his silence as a firm but fair consequence, the kind that would teach a lesson without shouting. Jake read it as rejection, as his father ceasing to see him at all, which hurt far more than any lecture would have.

He also read it through his own childhood. His father's silences had worked, in the sense that Gareth had obeyed. He had not stopped to ask what they had cost him.

And because Jake said nothing back, Gareth took the silence as working, when it was the silence of a boy who had concluded there was no point in speaking to his father.

His wife's warning also went unheard because Gareth had already decided what the silence was: a lesson. Once a reading becomes a principle, it is very hard to revise.
moreCases.betterRead:
Kipling Williams's research on ostracism, including the Cyberball studies in which people were simply left out of an online game of catch, shows that being ignored hurts quickly and deeply, even by strangers in a trivial game. Being ignored by a parent for days is a far more powerful version. The silent treatment communicates not "I am angry about what you did" but "you do not exist to me", and for a teenager that message can outweigh any lesson about lying. Jake's withdrawal and his conclusion that his father hated him were the predictable result. The better approach separates the consequence from the relationship. Gareth sat down with Jake that evening and said, "I've been angry, and I shouldn't have stopped talking to you. I don't hate you. I was frightened. Lying about where you are isn't OK, so you're not going out next weekend. And I want to know you're safe, so next time, tell me the truth and we'll sort it out." Jake cried again, and so, nearly, did Gareth.

Jake's mother told Gareth afterwards that it was the first time she had seen him apologise to their son.

moreCases.title: The colleague who needed five seconds
moreCases.scene:
Priya, thirty-four, joins a product team at a software firm. She is thoughtful and precise, and when she is asked a question in a meeting,
  she pauses before she answers: three seconds, sometimes five, her eyes moving slightly upward as she thinks. In her first few meetings, every time
  she pauses, someone else jumps in. The team lead, Mark, rephrases the question, or a colleague, Tom, answers it for her. By the third week, Priya has
  mostly stopped speaking in meetings.

  Mark notices that Priya's written comments on the project documents are the most insightful on the team. He wonders why she says so little in
  person, and asks her, at a one-to-one, whether she is finding the meetings difficult.

  Priya says that she likes to think before she speaks, and that by the time she is ready, someone has always already said something.

Priya also mentions that in her previous job, the team lead used to count to five after asking a question, and that she had not realised how much she depended on it until she moved.

Priya has also noticed that when she does manage to speak, people sometimes talk over the end of her sentences, as if they assumed she had finished because she paused. She has started speaking faster, which makes her less clear and more anxious.

Tom, who answers most often, is a fast talker who likes to keep meetings moving. He thinks of himself as helpful, and in many ways he is. He has never noticed that the meetings he keeps moving are the ones in which Priya says nothing.
moreCases.misread:
The team read Priya's pauses as hesitation, uncertainty or not knowing the answer, and filled them to help her. Each rescue told her that her silence was a problem, and that her turn was over before it had begun.

Tom's habit of answering for her, which he meant as helpful, also sent a message to the rest of the team: that Priya needed rescuing, which shaped how they treated her in other ways.

Mark himself had been part of it. He rephrased questions when Priya paused, believing he was being helpful, and never noticed that she had not needed help.

And the team never asked Priya what the pauses meant. They supplied their own explanation and acted on it every week.
moreCases.betterRead:
People vary a great deal in how long they need before they speak, and a pause before answering is often a sign of thought rather than uncertainty. Priya's upward glance and stillness during her pauses fit someone thinking hard, as the chapter on the gaze described in Glenberg's finding that people look away more when questions are difficult. In a fast-talking team, a five-second silence feels long, and the urge to fill it is strong. But filling it, however kindly meant, takes the turn away. Mark's better response was to change the team's habits. He told the team that he wanted to try waiting a few seconds longer after questions, and he modelled it himself, counting silently after asking Priya something and holding up a hand when Tom started to answer. Within a few weeks, Priya was speaking in every meeting, and two of her suggestions had changed the product's direction. Tom admitted that he had always assumed silence meant someone was stuck.

Priya also started telling new colleagues, in her first meeting with them, that she liked a moment to think, which made it easy for them to wait.

moreCases.title: The friend who went quiet on the phone
moreCases.scene:
Neil, fifty, rings his oldest friend, Graham, every Sunday evening. For twenty years the calls have been easy: football, work, family,
  arguments about politics. Over the winter, they change. Graham's answers get shorter. There are long gaps on the line, five, ten seconds, in which
  Neil can hear him breathing but he says nothing. When Neil asks how he is, Graham says "fine" after a pause, in a flat voice. Twice, Graham says he
  has to go after ten minutes.

  Neil starts to fill the gaps. He tells longer stories about his own week, asks more questions, makes more jokes. Graham laughs less each time.

  Neil's wife, listening from the kitchen one Sunday, says that Graham sounds exhausted, and that Neil is doing all the talking.

Neil has also noticed that Graham no longer argues about politics. For twenty years they have disagreed about almost everything, cheerfully. This winter, when Neil says something provocative, Graham just says, "Maybe."

Neil has also noticed that Graham no longer asks about Neil's children, which he always used to, or mentions his own. The calls have become, Neil realises, a monologue with occasional breathing on the other end.

When Neil mentioned the long gaps to his own brother, his brother said Graham was probably just bored of the calls. Neil half believed it, and the thought stung.
moreCases.misread:
Neil read the gaps on the line as awkwardness to be smoothed over, and his own stories as a way of keeping the friendship going. He did not ask himself which kind of silence he was hearing.

He also read the silence through his own discomfort with it. Filling the gaps made the calls feel normal to him, even as they told him less and less about his friend.

Graham, for his part, may have felt the gaps as relief. Each one Neil filled was a moment he did not have to perform being fine.

He also did not ask Graham about the silence itself. People are often relieved when someone names a change in them, because it means they no longer have to hide it.
moreCases.betterRead:
When a man falls silent, the question is which silence it is. On the phone, there is no face or posture to read, so the voice and the silence itself carry everything: the length of the gaps, the flatness of "fine", the absence of laughter, the shortening of the calls. Against twenty years of easy Sunday calls, those changes made a cluster that fitted exhaustion, low mood or something weighing on Graham far better than mere awkwardness. Filling the gaps kept the call going and kept Graham's state hidden. The better approach, which Neil tried the following week, was to ask about the silence itself and then to wait. He said, "You've been really quiet the last few weeks, mate. Not like you. What's going on?" Then he said nothing, for nearly half a minute. Graham said, eventually, that his work had been cut to three days and that he had not told his wife. They talked for an hour. The next week, Neil drove over to see him.

Neil also changed how he ran the Sunday calls. He asked one real question near the start and waited, rather than filling the first ten minutes with his own news.

workedReading.title: The quiet at the allotment
workedReading.scene:
Tom, sixty, has had the allotment next to Vic's for eleven years. Vic, seventy-two, is a talker: about seeds, weather, his late brother, the council's failings, anything. On Saturday mornings they work side by side and Vic talks almost continuously. This Saturday, Vic arrives late, digs for an hour without saying a word, and when Tom offers him a cup of tea from his flask, Vic shakes his head and keeps digging.

Tom likes Vic's talking, though he would never say so. It is part of the allotment: the birds, the soil, and Vic's running commentary on everything. The silence makes the morning feel strange.

The allotments are quiet this morning. A blackbird is singing somewhere, and the only other sound is the scrape of Vic's spade, harder and faster than Tom has ever heard it. Vic's thermos, which he always brings, is not on the bench by his shed.

Tom knows Vic's wife a little. Joan used to come to the allotment in summer with sandwiches and talk to everyone. He has not seen her there this year, and has not thought about it until now.

steps.label: Compare with the baseline
steps.text:
Tom's first observation is the size of the change. In eleven years he has rarely heard Vic stop talking for more than a few minutes. An hour of silence from this man is a large departure, and that alone makes it worth paying attention to, whatever it means.

He also notes that Vic arrived late, which he has done only once before, the week his brother died. Lateness and silence together are more informative than either alone.

He also remembers the last time Vic was quiet, the week after his brother's funeral. Then, Vic stayed at home for two weeks and came back thinner. This is the first long silence since then.

steps.label: Look at the breath and body
steps.text:
Tom glances across, as he would anyway, without staring. Vic's digging is harder and faster than usual. His breathing is heavy, more than the work requires. His jaw is set. He has not looked up from the soil since he arrived. This does not look like the comfortable silence of two men absorbed in work, with relaxed bodies and wandering eyes.

He also notes that Vic has not looked at his own vegetables, which he usually inspects first thing, talking to them as if they were children. Something has pushed even that aside.

He also notices that Vic's cap is pulled lower than usual, shading his eyes, and that he has not taken his coat off, though the digging is warm work. Small changes to a familiar picture.

steps.label: Consider the rivals
steps.text:
Tom runs through the possibilities. Vic could be tired or unwell. He could be angry about something, perhaps something Tom has done, though Tom cannot think what. He could be worried or grieving. He could simply have nothing to say today, which would be a first. The fierce digging and the refusal of tea point towards something weighing on him rather than mere fatigue.

He also checks whether he could be the cause. He last spoke to Vic on Wednesday, about the water butts, and it was friendly. Nothing since then seems likely to have caused this.

He also considers whether he should leave Vic alone. Some men want silence and space, and Tom does not want to intrude. He decides that one light remark, easily ignored, is the right balance.

steps.label: Test gently
steps.text:
Tom does not ask what is wrong straight away. He keeps working, side by side, and after a while says, lightly, "You're quiet today, Vic." Then he goes back to his own digging and waits. The remark names the silence without demanding an explanation, and it leaves Vic free to answer or not.

He also chooses a remark rather than a question, because a question demands an answer and a remark only invites one. "You're quiet today" can be answered with a nod, a word or the whole story.

He also keeps his tone light and his eyes on his own work as he says it, so that the remark feels like part of an ordinary morning rather than a summons to talk.

steps.label: Hold the silence
steps.text:
Vic does not answer for nearly a minute. Tom does not fill the gap. He keeps his own breath slow and his eyes on his own patch of ground. He reminds himself that many men need a silence before they can say something hard, and that the silence after his remark is part of the conversation, not the end of it.

He also notices the pull to add something, "Everything all right at home?", and lets it pass. One opening is enough; two can feel like being questioned.

He also notices that Vic's digging slows after the remark. The spade goes in more gently, twice, three times, and then stops. Tom takes the slowing as a sign that something is coming.

steps.label: Listen to what comes
steps.text:
Vic stops digging, leans on his spade and says, to the ground, that his wife, Joan, has been diagnosed with dementia. They found out on Thursday. He has not told anyone. Tom says, "Oh, Vic. I'm so sorry," and puts his own spade down. He does not ask questions straight away. He lets Vic say more, in his own time, and he does.

He also does not offer advice or information about dementia, though he knows a little about it from his own mother. That can wait for another day, if Vic wants it.

He also notices that Vic's breathing, which was heavy, has begun to slow now that he has said it. Saying it aloud seems to have let something go.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
They sit on the bench by Tom's shed for half an hour, mostly in silence, which feels different now: heavy, but shared. Vic has the tea after all. Before they leave, Vic says it helped to say it out loud. Tom notes, later, that if he had chattered to fill the quiet, as he was tempted to, Vic might have dug his way through the whole morning and gone home without saying it.

The following Saturday, Vic arrives on time and talks for most of the morning, and Tom has never been so glad to hear it.

Tom also starts bringing two cups in his flask on Saturdays, so that he can hand one over without asking. Vic takes it every week, and some weeks he talks about Joan, and some weeks he does not.

moreFailures.title: Treating silence as empty
moreFailures.body:
It is easy to think of silence as the absence of communication, a gap to be filled or ignored. Koudenburg and colleagues found that even a four-second silence in a conversation made people feel less self-assured and less like they belonged, sometimes without their noticing that it had happened. Silence always says something. Between strangers, it often signals awkwardness or rejection. Between close friends, it can signal comfort and trust. In an argument, it can signal flooding, contempt or punishment. In grief, it can signal respect. The first step in reading silence is to take it as seriously as speech.

It also helps to notice silences in writing. An unanswered message, a reply that comes a day late, a group chat in which someone has stopped posting: these are silences too, and they can be read in the same ways.

It also helps to notice the silences that follow particular topics. If a friend goes quiet every time his father is mentioned, the pattern tells you more than any single silence.

It also helps to notice how long silences have lasted in a relationship. A friendship in which nothing real has been said for years has its own silence, quieter and harder to see than a pause in a conversation.

moreFailures.title: Filling every silence
moreFailures.body:
The commonest mistake with silence is to fill it. Someone says something hard, or pauses before answering, and the listener rushes in with advice, reassurance, a story of his own or a rephrased question, because the silence feels unbearable. The person who was about to say more, or who was still thinking, stops. Many men need a silence before they can say what matters, and many thoughtful people need a few seconds before they speak. After you ask a real question, wait: count to ten in your head if you need to, keep your body still and your breath slow, and let the silence do its work.

It also helps to notice whose silences you fill. Many people fill the silences of women, younger colleagues and quieter men far more readily than those of senior or confident people.

It also helps to know that filling silence is often about the listener's anxiety, not the speaker's need. Noticing your own discomfort, and letting it be, is most of the skill.

It also helps to tell people that you will wait. "Take your time, there's no rush" makes the silence feel safe rather than awkward, and many people start talking soon after hearing it.

moreFailures.title: Misreading or leaving a stonewall
moreFailures.body:
When a partner goes silent in an argument, still-faced, looking away, no longer responding, it is easy to read it as contempt or indifference and to push harder. Gottman's research suggests that stonewalling often comes with flooding: a racing heart and an overwhelmed body that cannot keep engaging. Pushing makes it worse. If you are the one going silent, the opposite failure is to leave the other person shut out, without explanation. Name it: "I'm flooding. I need twenty minutes, and then I'll come back." Then come back, as Martin learned to do.

It also helps to agree on the signal in advance, as Martin and Claire did. A word or a phrase that means "I'm flooding" is much easier to say in the moment than a full explanation.

It also helps to know that both people can flood. If you notice your own heart racing and your thoughts narrowing as your partner goes silent, you may need the break as much as they do.

It also helps to remember that partners who stonewall are often the ones who feel the conflict most intensely, not least. The stillness can be a sign of how much is going on inside, not how little.

moreFailures.title: Using silence as punishment
moreFailures.body:
Refusing to speak to someone for hours or days, as a way of showing displeasure, is one of the most painful things one person can do to another. Williams's research on ostracism shows how quickly being ignored hurts, even by strangers in a trivial game. From a partner or a parent, it can feel like being erased. It also teaches nothing useful, because the person on the receiving end often does not know what they did, or how to put it right. If you need time to calm down, say so, and say when you will talk. If a consequence is needed, say it in words. Silence used as a weapon damages the relationship more than the original offence.

Children are particularly affected by parental silence. Many adults remember the silent treatment from their childhood more vividly than any shouting, and say it left them anxious about silence for the rest of their lives.

In workplaces, a manager who ignores someone, stops copying them into emails or leaves them out of meetings is using a form of ostracism, and it can be as damaging there as at home.

And if you have used silence this way, it is worth saying so afterwards. "I shouldn't have stopped talking to you" is a simple repair that many people never hear.

questions.q: Why do silences feel so uncomfortable?
questions.a:
Partly because conversation usually flows with very short gaps between turns, so a longer gap stands out, and partly because silence is ambiguous. Koudenburg and colleagues found that even a four-second silence made people feel less confident and less like they belonged. In most conversations, silence raises a question, about whether you have said something wrong, whether the other person is bored, whether the relationship is all right, and people rush to answer it by speaking. Knowing this can help you sit with a silence a little longer, and recognise that the discomfort is yours, not necessarily a sign that anything is wrong.

It also helps to know that comfort with silence varies between people, families and cultures. A family that talks constantly may read a silence as a crisis; a family that is often quiet may barely notice it.

It also helps to notice silences on video calls, which are often made worse by lag. A two-second delay can make a pause feel longer than it is, and people talk over each other trying to fill it.

It may also help to remember that silence can be a gift. Leaving room for someone else to speak, or simply to be, is one of the kindest things a listener can do.

questions.q: How long should I wait after asking a hard question?
questions.a:
Longer than feels comfortable. Many people need several seconds, and some need much longer, before they can answer a question that matters, especially men answering questions about feelings, and thoughtful people answering complex questions in meetings. Counting slowly to ten in your head is a useful habit: by the time you reach it, the other person has often begun to speak. Keep your body still and near, your breath slow, and your eyes somewhere other than their face if you are side by side. If nothing comes after a long wait, you can say, gently, "Take your time," or "We don't have to talk about it now."

It may also help to give a sign that you are not going anywhere, such as staying seated, keeping your hands still or making a small, warm sound. The other person can then take their time without worrying that you will leave.

It also helps to watch for signs that the person is about to speak: an intake of breath, a slight lift of the head, lips parting. Those are signs to keep waiting, not to step in.

questions.q: What do people mean by flooding?
questions.a:
Flooding is Gottman's term for a state of physiological overwhelm during conflict: the heart races, breathing quickens, thinking narrows, and the person feels unable to take in or respond to what is being said. People who are flooded often go silent and still, which is what stonewalling looks like from outside, and they may feel an urge to escape. Gottman's advice is that a flooded person needs a break, of at least twenty minutes, spent doing something genuinely calming rather than rehearsing the argument, before the conversation can usefully continue. Saying so, rather than just going silent, makes the break a pause rather than a rejection.

It also helps to know that flooding is not a choice and not a weakness. Some people flood more easily than others, often because of temperament or past experience, and knowing your own pattern makes it easier to manage.

It also helps to agree with your partner, at a calm time, what each of you will do during a break, so that the twenty minutes is spent calming down rather than preparing the next round.

questions.q: Is the silent treatment a form of abuse?
questions.a:
It can be. An occasional sulk after an argument is a common, if unhelpful, part of many relationships. But silence used repeatedly and deliberately to punish, control or frighten someone, lasting days, withdrawn as a reward for compliance, or used alongside other controlling behaviour, is recognised by many professionals as a form of emotional abuse. The difference lies in its purpose and pattern: a time-out says "I need space and I'll be back"; the silent treatment says "you don't exist until you give me what I want". If you are on the receiving end of the second kind, talk to someone you trust, and consider the support services described in the chapter on anger.

It also helps to notice your own pattern. If you find yourself using silence to punish, it is worth asking what you want the other person to understand, and saying that instead.

If you are the one using the silent treatment, it can help to ask what you are afraid would happen if you spoke. Often the silence protects the person using it from saying something they fear they would regret.

questions.q: How can I tell whether a friend's silence is comfortable?
questions.a:
Watch the body and the breath. In a comfortable silence, bodies are relaxed and still, breathing is slow and even, both people tend to look at the same thing or at nothing in particular, and when they do look at each other, it is easy. Hands are loose. Small movements, such as shifting position or adjusting a fishing line, are unhurried. In an uncomfortable or troubled silence, you may see a braced or collapsed posture, held or shallow breathing, a fixed stare, fidgeting or eyes that avoid yours. If you are not sure, a light remark, such as "Nice to just sit, isn't it?", usually gets a response that tells you which it is.

It also helps to notice how long the silence lasts and how it ends. A comfortable silence usually ends easily, with a remark or a smile; a troubled one often ends abruptly, or not at all.

It also helps to notice how you feel in the silence. If it feels restful, it probably is. If it feels like holding your breath, something may be unsaid.

It also helps to accept that comfortable silence takes time to build. Two people who have only just met will rarely feel it, however much they like each other.

questions.q: What if I am the quiet one?
questions.a:
Then it can help to explain your silences, because others will otherwise supply their own explanations, often unflattering ones. A simple sentence does a great deal: "I'm quiet because I'm thinking, not because I disagree," or "I'm not a big talker, but I'm enjoying this." In meetings, it can help to say that you would like a moment to think before you answer, so that people know to wait. In arguments, if you go quiet because you are flooding, say so and say when you will come back. Being quiet is not a flaw. Being misread because nobody knows why you are quiet is a problem you can solve with a few words.

It also helps to choose settings that suit you. Many quiet people find that walks, drives and shared tasks, where silence is natural, make it easier to talk when they want to.

It may also help to notice when you go quiet with some people and not others. Silence that comes only with one person may be telling you something about that relationship.

It also helps to know that quiet people are often excellent listeners and observers, and that teams and families benefit from making room for them.

watch.title: A Beautiful Day in the Neighborhood: I Don't Think You Are Broken
watch.notice: Fred Rogers, played by Tom Hanks, talks with a cynical journalist. Notice his pauses: how long he lets silence sit, and what it draws out of the other man.

reviewPrompt: This week, after one real question, count to ten before speaking, and explain one of your own silences that might be misread.
